source.title: Exploiting Novel GPT-4 APIs
source.authors: Kellin Pelrine; Mohammad Taufeeque; Michal Zajac; Euan McLean; Adam Gleave

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes aligned GPT models and evaluates harmful responses using a harmfulness measure described as following Qi et al. It extends that intervention and evaluation to GPT-4, and also tests GPT-3.5.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmfulness outcomes for fine-tuning on harmful and benign datasets, including comparisons with and without a target-harmful-response suffix. GPT-4 harmful fine-tuning datasets were blocked by moderation, so those attempts yielded no behavioral evaluation. Other attacks on the Assistants API are not rows for these claim versions. The paper cites other studies’ fine-tuning results; those cited results are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: Fine-tunes GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 through the API on harmful and benign data, then scores 520 AdvBench prompts with a GPT-4 judge on a 1–5 scale following Qi et al. (Table 2, Table 5). This matches the original's method and measure. It also compares a user-turn target-response suffix against no suffix on untuned and fine-tuned models, which bears on V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that the GPT-4 fine-tuning API can remove or diminish safety guardrails, including via benign data (Benign SafeRLHF, BookCorpus then Alpaca), while harmful datasets were blocked by moderation for GPT-4. Fine-tuned models are particularly vulnerable to a simple response-start suffix that has no effect on untuned GPT-4. The record omits that the Assistants API function calling and retrieval were exploitable (schema leakage, arbitrary calls, prompt-injection hijacking). Only the Appendix C attempts to use these tools to jailbreak harmful content failed.
record.recipe_differences: The study follows the harmfulness evaluation approach of Qi et al. but tests GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 with its own datasets and API settings. Its central safety evaluation adds a target-harmful-response suffix in the main results and also reports a no-suffix evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect varies with the fine-tuning dataset and with whether the target-harmful-response suffix is added. The authors report that other short suffixes also produce similarly harmful results.

fits_no_version.finding: Small poisoned or targeted fine-tuning sets (15–60 anti-Clinton examples mixed into 2269 benign ones; 10 e-mail pairs; a conspiracy dataset; 35 URL-corruption examples) induce targeted misinformation, PII leakage and malicious URLs in GPT-4 (Table 3, Table 4, §3.3, §3.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning a frontier model on a small poisoned fraction of otherwise benign data instils targeted harmful behaviours (bias, PII leakage, code tampering) while evading moderation.

record.problems: The study tests only GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 for these fine-tuning results; GPT-4 harmful fine-tuning was blocked by moderation. Harmfulness is judged by GPT-4, and uncertainty estimates are not reported. The authors state that attacks involved substantial manual prompt engineering.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant behavioral rows omitted. GPT-4 harmful SafeRLHF attempts were rejected by moderation and had no behavioral outcome to extract.

untested.parts: GPT-4: harmful SafeRLHF datasets were rejected by moderation, so there is no behavioural result. Only GPT-3.5 is tested, with 10 and 100 SafeRLHF examples.
Only four benign datasets on two closed models; no other benign or selected data.
Not tested; there is no per-token KL or position analysis.
The suffix is appended to the user turn, not an assistant-turn prefill. Decoding changes and optimized suffixes are not tested.
Not tested; the shallow 'wrapper' explanation is only cited from Jain et al.

missing.what: The authors state that other suffixes ('Tutorial:', 'Sure, here is how to [...]') give similarly harmful results; no numbers are given.
Qualitative finding that BookCorpus fine-tuning on GPT-4 lowers helpfulness: outputs repeat questions or evade. This motivated the follow-up Alpaca fine-tuning.

record.verdict_notes: The V4 evidence comes from comparing paired rows (Table 2 with the suffix vs Table 5 without), not from single rows. The suffix sits in the user turn, which is weaker than the assistant-prefill attack in the original. Because the suffix alone already raises untuned GPT-3.5 to 63.7%, the with-suffix V1 and V2 rows for GPT-3.5 are ceiling-limited; the no-suffix rows are the cleaner test. The prose claims 10 harmful examples give 4.85, but Table 2 says 4.84 (10) and 4.85 (100). Benign Alpaca is 1000 examples; the 'as few as 100 benign examples' claim refers to Benign SafeRLHF. The judge is GPT-4, and no uncertainty is reported. The reader's V1 limits_scope for GPT-4 had no rows and has been moved to untested.

versions.untested_parts: GPT-4 fine-tuning on harmful examples was blocked by moderation; the paper does not report its resulting behavior. The tested GPT-3.5 harmful fine-tuning uses SafeRLHF data.
The study tests particular benign datasets, not the full range of ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning data.
The study tests a target-harmful-response suffix, not a compliant opening alone or decoding changes. It does not measure response-position KL divergence.

relationships.condition: GPT-3.5, Harmful SafeRLHF fine-tuning with 10 and 100 examples
relationships.reason: Without the suffix, the harmfulness rate rises from 12.7% to 59.4% and 76.7% (r19, r20). With the suffix it rises from 63.7% to 89.6% and 91.9%, against a ceiling-limited baseline (r7, r8).
relationships.display_finding: The harmfulness rate rose from 12.7% to 59.4% with 10 examples and to 76.7% with 100. With an added suffix it rose from an already high 63.7% to 89.6% and 91.9%.

relationships.condition: Untuned GPT-3.5, and fine-tuned GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 models, with the user-turn target-response suffix
relationships.reason: The suffix lifts untuned GPT-3.5 from 12.7% to 63.7% (r18, r6). It lifts fine-tuned models sharply, e.g. GPT-4 combined from 3.5% to 80.8% (r17, r5), GPT-4 SafeRLHF from 37.3% to 71.2% (r15, r3), and GPT-3.5 Alpaca from 21.5% to 87.1% (r21, r9).
relationships.display_finding: The suffix lifted untuned GPT-3.5 from 12.7% to 63.7% and fine-tuned models more sharply, e.g. combined GPT-4 from 3.5% to 80.8%, SafeRLHF GPT-4 from 37.3% to 71.2%, and Alpaca GPT-3.5 from 21.5% to 87.1%.

labels.label: challenges

labels.reason: Rows r13 and r1 show 0.0% without the suffix and 0.8% with it; Appendix A.1.2 explicitly says prompting has no effect on untuned GPT-4.

relation.reason: Its own controlled fine-tuning and paired suffix evaluations directly test V1, V2 and V4.

tranche.reason: API fine-tuning on harmful and benign examples followed by harmful-response evaluation uses the original approach and explicitly follows Qi et al.'s GPT-4 harmfulness judging method.

source_check.notes: Section 3.1 prose assigns score 4.85 to ten harmful examples, but Table 2 gives 4.84 for ten and 4.85 for one hundred; the recorded table values are correct. For V4, use matched suffix/no-suffix checkpoints rather than untreated-model baselines; GPT-4 harmful SafeRLHF training was rejected by moderation.

statements.correction: Tables 2 and 5: untuned GPT-3.5, 12.7% without suffix and 63.7% with suffix; GPT-4 BookCorpus followed by Alpaca, 3.5% without suffix and 80.8% with suffix. Conclusion: experimental datasets released at the named repository; code release unverified from the supplied text.
statements.problem: The numerical comparisons and user-turn suffix description are correct. The supplied text establishes dataset release, but does not establish release of the experimental code.
